layer0_index.name: Section Six: Selection, Tapping, Luncheons, Initiation
layer0_index.description: How members are selected, tapping ceremonies, luncheons, initiation, and the feminist challenge.
layer0_index.one_sentence_summary: Section Six: Selection, Tapping, Luncheons, Initiation: How members are selected, tapping ceremonies, luncheons, initiation, and the feminist challenge. (6 subsections)

layer1_summary.paragraph: The rituals, ceremonies, and evolving standards surrounding how Iron Arrow selects and initiates its members form the organizational heartbeat of the society, reflecting both its Seminole-inspired ideals and its ongoing struggle to remain relevant across changing campus climates. The transition away from Doc Adams's era forced the tribe to codify unwritten traditions and substantially reimagine its initiation, while external pressures — from campus unrest to feminist challenges — tested the society's identity and resilience. Understanding these processes reveals how Iron Arrow continuously negotiated between honoring its founding traditions and adapting to an evolving university community.
bullets: The retirement of Thurston "Doc" Adams as Director of Student Activities in the late 1960s left Iron Arrow without its institutional anchor, forcing a small group of student leaders including John Leatherwood, Martin Arostegui, and Michael Tryson to formalize unwritten customs before they disappeared entirely.

The selection process came under severe strain during the Vietnam era, when campus unrest, drug use, and administrative indifference made it uncertain whether enough qualified candidates even existed to tap, yet leaders were found and the tribe emerged stronger for the ordeal.

The physical initiation ceremony was deliberately moved from Lake Osceola into the Everglades after 1967 to eliminate hazing elements and deepen the ritual's connection to Seminole traditions and the Florida wilderness.

Medicine Man Mike Tryson's 1968 discovery of a newspaper clipping describing the Seminole Wheel of Life became the seed of a transformed initiation ritual, one that embedded genuine indigenous symbolism at the ceremony's core.

Continuity during the turbulent "Micco Years" was preserved largely through extended chieftainships — John Leatherwood served three years, Rhea Warren and John Benedict two years each — providing seven years of combined stable leadership when no other source of continuity existed.

layer2_details.text:
SELECTION

- Selection process was subject to repeated external assault from "outraged aspirants whose ambitions went unfulfilled" who launched "repeated, rather spectacular assaults upon the tribe itself, and especially on the 'one-ball' system"
- Hurricane (student newspaper) ran headlines, columns, and editorials criticizing organizations with selective membership procedures, social or honorary
- John Leatherwood made lifting the selection process "above all reproach, real or imagined" one of his first objectives beginning in 1969
- Constitutional revision aimed to "provide a strict constitutional selection procedure to remove any possibility of a political misuse of the 'ball', while retaining the founding principle of unanimity and preventing a decline in the standards required for Iron Arrow membership"
- Revised procedures came "perilously close to becoming a 'two-ball' system" but ultimately set aside forever "the potential for a political or personal grudge exercise of the negative vote"
- Son of Chief was designated coordination responsibilities for the selection and tapping of new members under the constitutional redefinition of officer duties
- During the late 1960s, selection meetings were held in which "it was wondered if there would be anyone even eligible to tap, much less desirable"
- Renewed notoriety and respect for the tribe was partly due to adjusted selection procedures and partly to the personality and public-relations emphasis of individual Chiefs

TAPPING

- Tapping of new members was coordinated by the Son of Chief under the revised constitutional structure
- Leaders continued to be tapped even during the turbulent Micco years, which "only served to forge a stronger, more permanent place for the Arrow"
- Among the last tappees from the Thurston Adams years: John Leatherwood, Martin Arostegui, Michael Tryson, Michael Leone, Stephen Hill, Thad Koch, Tim Choate, Steve Haas, and the author (of the history)

TAPPING LUNCHEONS

- The Chief was assigned specific responsibility for the tapping luncheons and their arrangements under the constitutional revision of the Micco years
- Dr. Henry King Stanford and Mrs. Stanford hosted a Homecoming reception for Iron Arrow members and guests each year, first held October 27, 1971, at the old W. T. Grant mansion on South Bayshore Drive in Coconut Grove — home of the first three presidents of the University
- The Stanford Homecoming reception tradition continued at President and Mrs. Stanford's new home on Old Cutler Road near Matheson Hammock Park

THE INITIATION

- For most of Iron Arrow's history, initiation was held on campus around Lake Osceola; trips to wilderness areas occurred only as a finale, "devised more for 'hazing' new members than for examining the elements and significance of leadership"
- A revised printed version of the initiation ritual was drawn up by Barry Scott Richard, Chief 1966–67
- Construction of the 960 and 1968 dorms on the shores of Lake Osceola in 1967 and 1968 made moving the entire ceremony into the Everglades increasingly necessary
- Dissatisfaction existed with both physical hazing activities and the "comparatively shallow Seminole or Indian perspectives in much of the ceremony"
- In September or October 1968, Medicine Man Mike Tryson obtained a newspaper clipping briefly outlining the shape and skeletal symbolism of the Seminole Wheel of Life
- A James Hutchinson canvas depicts the Seminole Wheel of Life as drawn by Medicine Man Gotch Nagoftee, Josie Billie (footnote 112)
- In February 1969, the author boarded a Delta Airlines jet for an ODK Province Convention in Columbia, South Carolina; the Wheel of Life portion of the ritual was composed in the first 30 minutes of the flight and was finished by the time the flight landed in Atlanta
- The scene described was a wilderness area that Thad Koch had shown the author several weeks earlier, seen in daytime; the author wrote picturing it at night with a council fire and the Wheel of Life painted on the earth
- The Lessons in the Wilderness were added later that same spring, after the spring initiation; composed with difficulty, partly in an apartment in South Miami belonging to Iron Arrow member Steven Haas
- William Vaught, Associate Director of Student Activities and longtime Iron Arrow member, discussed with the author the use of symbolism in initiation ceremonies of Greek and Professional Societies, prompting research into several books on Indian cultures in North America including two or three on the Seminoles and their language
- Parts of the Lessons in the Wilderness were written with specific members of the tribe in mind, reflecting differing styles of leadership
- Seminole language was put to unofficial use as a result of the undertaking; member Ted Peck, Chairman of the 1968 Carni Gras, was known at tribal functions as Empeshaw, the Seminole word for stomach
- The Medicine Man was specified as administrative domain holder for the initiation ritual and the subsequent breakfast under the constitutional revision
- The initiation ritual and the subsequent breakfast were specified as the administrative domain of the Medicine Man

THE FEMINIST CHALLENGE

- No content on the Feminist Challenge was present in the provided source text excerpt

BITS AND PIECES

- Thurston "Doc" Adams's retirement as Director of Student Activities marked the end of nearly two decades of experience upon which the tribe had grown dependent; he left no heir-apparent
- The Micco years (1968–1976) were named for the dominance of long-reigning Chiefs: John Leatherwood served three years; Rhea Warren and John Benedict each served two years — seven years of continuity among them
- John Leatherwood's "audacious representation of the tribe and all its traditions created an aura of theatric prestige that soon surrounded Iron Arrow with a sense of its own majesty"; his repeated elections attributed more to "his overpowering sense of presence on the campus stage than to considerations of platform or program"
- Unwritten traditions, gradual and accumulated revisions, and word-of-mouth experiences were "all in danger of disappearing quickly and irretrievably" after Doc Adams's departure
- The constitutional revision also redefined duties of tribal officers in more pragmatic terms: the Chief was given responsibility for coordination of all tribal activities plus specific responsibility for tapping luncheons; the Son of Chief coordinated selection and tapping; the Medicine Man administered the initiation ritual and breakfast
- Recognition for establishing the University of Miami fund connecting the university community with Everglades tribes is due: Eugene Cohen, Dr. Stanford, John J. DuPuis Jr., and Charlton Tebeau
